title: Classify a Diagnostic Fault Code (MISRA Switch Rules)
statement:
A fault code coming off a bus, a diagnostic connector or an internal fault
table only means something once it is mapped to a severity: something a
warning lamp, a logger or a shutdown sequence can act on without knowing
what any individual code stands for.

This one is written to **MISRA C:2012**, the same way the Linear
Interpolation Over a Calibration Table problem is. Nothing here runs a
static analyser over your submission -- the tests only check behaviour --
but the reference solution follows the switch-statement rules below, and
matching them is the point of the exercise.

## Your function

```
int32_t classify_fault(int32_t code);
```

Codes are documented one at a time, not as ranges:

- `0` -- no fault -- severity `0`
- `101`, `102`, `103` -- sensor faults (coolant temp, MAF, O2) -- severity `1`
- `201`, `202` -- actuator faults (injector circuit, fuel pump circuit) -- severity `2`
- `301` -- brake actuator fault -- severity `3`

Return the documented severity for a code in that list. For any code that is
**not** on it -- including negative codes and codes that merely look close
to a real one -- return `-1`.

## The MISRA rules this problem is built around

- **Rule 16.4 -- every `switch` shall have a `default` clause.** The list
  above is not exhaustive over all of `int32_t`; almost every value passed
  in is not a documented code. `default` is where those land, and it is not
  optional.
- **Rule 16.3 -- every `switch` clause ends with an unconditional `break`.**
  No clause falls through into the next by accident. Stacking bare case
  labels with nothing between them (`case 101: case 102: case 103:`) is not
  a violation of this rule -- there is no statement to fall through past --
  but a clause that runs code and then omits its `break` is.
- **Rule 15.5 (advisory) -- a function should have a single point of exit.**
  Assign to a result variable inside the `switch` and return it once, after
  the `switch` ends, rather than returning directly from inside each case.

## Watch out

- **This is not a range check, and implementing it as one is the trap.** It
  is tempting to write `if (code >= 100 && code < 200) severity = 1;` instead
  of enumerating `101`, `102` and `103` -- fewer lines, looks equivalent. It
  is not: `150` is inside that range and is not a documented code. A fixed
  test queries exactly this gap. Enumerate the documented codes; do not infer
  a pattern from their spacing.
- **A `switch` without a `default`, combined with a single point of exit,
  is worse than either mistake alone.** If no case matches and there is no
  `default`, the result variable that the final `return` reads is never
  written -- the function returns an indeterminate value instead of failing
  in an obvious way. Rule 16.4's mandatory `default` is what closes that gap.

tests.name: every documented code returns its documented severity
tests.description: One query per row of the table, in table order.

tests.name: a code between two real ones is unknown, not a nearby severity
tests.description: 150 sits between the 101-103 sensor codes and the 201-202 actuator codes but is not itself documented -- a range-based implementation would wrongly accept it.

tests.name: a negative code does not crash and is treated as unknown
a code just past the last documented one is still unknown
repeated queries in one run are classified independently
